kiryas-joel.story:
Kiryas Joel is a village in New York whose people are Satmar Hasidim, who practise a strict form of Judaism. Its founders drew its boundaries under New York's general village incorporation law so as to take in only Satmars. Its children attended religious schools, but children with disabilities needed special public services, and the village fell within the Monroe-Woodbury Central School District. In 1989 New York's legislature passed Chapter 748, a special statute that carved out a separate public school district following the village's lines.

Taxpayers sued, and in 1994 the United States Supreme Court ruled the statute unconstitutional under the First Amendment's bar on establishing a religion. Justice Souter said the district had not received its authority as one of many communities eligible under a general law, so there was no assurance that the next religious community would get the same treatment. Four justices also said that handing state authority over public schools to a group defined by common religion brought about a fusion of government and religion, comparing the case to Larkin v. Grendel's Den. The Court pointed out that other means of serving those children existed.

The decision did not overturn the village, which was formed under the general law. The case therefore draws a line between a community that uses general rules open to anyone and a government that writes a special law for one faith. Founders of a religious community meet that line whenever they ask a legislature for something of their own.

The dispute went on after the ruling, because New York's legislature kept rewriting the law. The litigation passed between the state courts and the United States Supreme Court for 12 years. It ended in 2001, when a state court upheld the legislature's fourth law devised to allow such a district. Early in 2002 the Kiryas Joel Union Free School District joined the state's association of school boards, which had been its leading opponent in court. So the 1994 ruling struck down one statute, and the same community later obtained its district under a different one.
kiryas-joel.why: Outcome missing: the entry stopped at 1994 as court-defeated, but litigation ran 12 years and a state court upheld a fourth law in 2001, so the district exists. Status and end changed; caller may prefer to keep the 1994 end date.

add_sources.t: Tamar Lewin, Controversy Over, Enclave Joins School Board Group, New York Times, 20 Apr 2002 (University of Maryland copy)

palapa-westar-recovery.story:
Earlier in 1984 the Space Shuttle mission STS-41-B released two communications satellites, Palapa B2 and Westar 6. Their kick motors, which were meant to raise them to high orbit, malfunctioned and left them stranded in the wrong orbits. Ground controllers lowered them from about 970 kilometres to about 340 kilometres so that a shuttle could reach them. In November 1984 the shuttle Discovery, on mission STS-51-A, met them.

On the fifth day of the mission the astronauts Joseph Allen and Dale Gardner went outside, caught Palapa B2 with a device inserted in its motor nozzle, and brought it into the payload bay. They recovered Westar 6 on 14 November, two days after Palapa B2. Gardner held up a "For Sale" sign. Both came back to Earth, and Westar 6 was later sold to AsiaSat, a company based in Hong Kong.

This is the closest thing in space history to a salvage, and it appears to have worked because the people with rights in the satellites wanted them back. No dispute over title is recorded. Article VIII of the Outer Space Treaty says that ownership of a space object is not affected by its presence in space or by its return to Earth, and space lawyers say there is no right of salvage comparable to the one at sea.

So the mission does not show that anyone may take a dead satellite. It shows that a dead satellite can be recovered and resold when the owner agrees, and that the hardware then has a new life on Earth under ordinary property law.
palapa-westar-recovery.why: 'The next day' is wrong against the mission's spacewalk dates, 12 and 14 November 1984. The Wikipedia prose says 'a day later' but its own spacewalk table gives these dates.

shanghai-international-settlement.story:
The Shanghai International Settlement was a district of Shanghai governed for nearly a century by foreign residents. After Britain's victory in the First Opium War, the Treaty of Nanking opened five Chinese ports, including Shanghai, and Land Regulations agreed in 1845 between a Chinese official and the British consul set the first British settlement. In 1854 Western businessmen formed the Shanghai Municipal Council, against consular protests. New Land Regulations of 11 July 1854 said in Article 28 that the land remained Chinese territory, subject to China's sovereign rights. In 1863 the British settlement and the neighbouring American one merged, and the merged area is what became known as the International Settlement.

The council ran police, fire services, public works and, by the 1880s, utilities. Foreign taxpayers elected it, and property requirements meant only about 3 percent of the population could stand. Chinese residents could not join until 1928. Foreigners from treaty powers fell under their own national laws and consular courts, while Chinese people and citizens of non-treaty powers went before a Mixed Court from 1864 until 1926 and later other courts. A Volunteer Corps served as a reserve, and a British battalion arrived in 1927. The area reached 5,584 acres by 1899 and 22.59 square kilometres by 1925, with 1,137,298 people that year.

It ended through war and treaties. Japanese troops occupied it on 8 December 1941. Early in 1943 Britain and the United States gave up their rights by treaties with Chiang Kai-shek's Nationalist government, which could not be carried out while Japan held the city. In July 1943 Japan handed the council to the pro-Japanese Wang Jingwei government. The treaties took practical effect only after Japan's surrender in 1945, and a Liquidation Commission then met to settle the remaining details of the handover. It was the most developed case of private citizens running a city under a foreign treaty, and it depended on unequal treaties and on the armed force of the powers that imposed them.
shanghai-international-settlement.why: Added the 1863 merger that created the Settlement proper and the 1945 ending. 'February 1943' softened to 'early 1943': the source gives both wordings, and the treaties are generally dated January 1943.

hatton-rockall-shelf.story:
The Hatton-Rockall area is a stretch of shallow seabed in the North Atlantic, west of Ireland and Scotland. Rockall itself is a tiny rock that has drawn founders and protesters, including Tom McClean in 1985 and Greenpeace's Global State of Waveland in 1997. The seabed around it matters for a different reason, because four states claim it as continental shelf beyond 200 nautical miles. An Irish minister set out the position in a written answer to parliament in June 2019.

Ireland and the United Kingdom agreed on the boundary between their shares in 1988, and that agreement said the location of Rockall was irrelevant to where the boundary ran. Iceland and Denmark, acting for the Faroe Islands, do not accept their claims beyond 200 nautical miles and have made their own. Ireland and the United Kingdom filed submissions with the UN Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf in March 2009, which met Ireland's May 2009 deadline. Denmark filed in 2010.

Iceland has not filed. The Commission does not review submissions covering disputed areas without the consent of all states concerned. Iceland does not consent, so the submissions are on hold. The four countries have met regularly since 2001 to try to resolve the overlap and have not reached agreement. This is a useful picture of an unresolved shelf. The water above beyond 200 miles stays high seas, as UNCLOS says.

The floor is claimed four ways, and the expert process that could fix the limits cannot start. A founder might see an unfinished map. The treaty points the other way, since Article 77 says shelf rights do not depend on occupation or proclamation, so the seabed is treated as belonging to whichever state's claim proves good. A newcomer on the bottom would therefore have four governments with reason to object.
hatton-rockall-shelf.why: Added that the 1988 agreement expressly set the rock aside, which supports the entry's point that the shelf dispute does not turn on Rockall.

rwanda-cinnamon-filing.story:
On 21 September 2021 Rwanda's government submitted a filing to the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), the UN agency that coordinates radio use, for two satellite constellations named CINNAMON-217 and CINNAMON-937. The larger had 27 orbital shells with a total of 327,320 satellites, and the smaller was a subset with seven shells and 52,080. A filing is an early notice that a country plans to use certain frequencies and orbits.

An earlier filing, ANTON-1N0, had been made on 20 August 2021 under the name of Marvel Space Communications Co, and it was not successful. The Rwandan statement said such filings are essential to secure the possibility of future launches, and that it planned to become a hub for the African space industry. Rwanda launched its first satellite, RwaSat-1, in 2019 with help from Japan, and it passed a law creating a space agency in 2021.

What Rwanda intended with the filing was unclear at the time, and some linked it to a private company or to its investment in OneWeb. Later reports tied the filings to Greg Wyler, a satellite entrepreneur, and his company E-Space, by then based in Toulouse, France. In June 2023 E-Space told the trade publication Advanced Television that a further filing it had made through France, for 116,640 satellites, was in addition to its filings in Rwanda, and the publication reported that the Rwandan filings remained active. E-Space had launched three demonstration satellites on Rocket Lab vehicles in May 2022.

The case shows the reach of a small state's rights at the ITU, which treats every member alike, in the same way that Tonga's slot filings did from the 1980s, and it shows a private company reaching those rights through a willing state. It also shows the limits. Rwanda has only signed the Outer Space Treaty, the Rescue Agreement and the Liability Convention, according to the UN's table of 1 January 2026, and it has not joined the Registration Convention.

A filing does not put anything in orbit, does not register any object, and gives no one a place to live. Whether any of these satellites will ever fly is not known.
rwanda-cinnamon-filing.why: The filing's backer is reported: E-Space and Greg Wyler. Also the UN table shows Rwanda as a signatory of the Rescue Agreement too.

add_sources.t: Wyler now involved with 400,000+ satellites, Advanced Television, 30 Jun 2023

titan-oceangate-unregistered.story:
Titan was a small submersible built by the American company OceanGate and operated through its Bahamas subsidiary to carry paying passengers to the wreck of the Titanic, 372 nautical miles south-southeast of Cape Race in Newfoundland. It imploded on a dive on 18 June 2023 with five people on board, and all five died. It claimed no independence, and it matters here as the clearest modern example of a crewed vessel working in open ocean with no flag. The Transportation Safety Board of Canada set out the position in its report M23A0169. "The Titan and the LARS were not registered in any country", the report says, the LARS being the launch and recovery system.

They were not certified by any maritime authority or classification society. OceanGate had begun registering the first version of the craft in the Bahamas in August 2019, and it did not pursue that after learning the requirements. The Bahamas requires crewed submersibles to be registered, classed and in line with its rules. The dive site lay beyond Canada's 200-nautical-mile zone. The report notes that Canadian registration rules cover Canadian vessels everywhere and vessels in Canadian waters or its zone, and that Canada has no comprehensive rules for building or operating crewed submersibles.

International guidance, the International Maritime Organization's Circular 981, is not binding. The support ship, Polar Prince, was Canadian-flagged and classed. So a regulated ship launched an unregulated craft from a place where no coastal state had authority. The board found that the carbon fibre hull's real strength had never been validated and that it likely failed progressively, with damage building up on each dive until it imploded. It also found that the lack of outside oversight raised the risk to those involved. The report says UNCLOS requires ships to be registered in a single state. The board made six recommendations. Among them, it recommended that Canada set criteria for overseeing commercial vessels not registered or captured by port inspections, press the International Maritime Organization to make the guidance binding, and require submersibles operating with a Canadian support ship to comply.

These are aimed at the support ship, because that is where a state can reach. The case shows that having no flag can last for years in practice, and that no one aboard gained any protection from it.
titan-oceangate-unregistered.why: Story never said five people died or why the hull failed, both in the listed report; the board issued six recommendations, and the operator was a Bahamas subsidiary.

chagos-treaty-2025.story:
The Chagos Archipelago is a group of islands in the Indian Ocean. In 1965, before Mauritius became independent, Britain separated it from Mauritius to create the British Indian Ocean Territory. The Prime Minister told the Mauritian premier he could go home with independence or without it, and the Mauritian side accepted detachment for £3 million and promises that the islands would return when no longer needed. About 1,360 people lived there at the time. The UN General Assembly had asked Britain not to divide Mauritius, by a vote of 89 to none.

In February 2019 the International Court of Justice advised, 13 to 1, that decolonisation had not been lawfully completed and that Britain should end its administration as rapidly as possible. The court held that Mauritius could not validly consent to the detachment while under British authority, and that the separation had not rested on the free and genuine will of the people.

On 22 May 2025 the two prime ministers signed an agreement. Mauritius would hold sovereignty over the whole archipelago and would authorise Britain to use its rights over Diego Garcia, the site of a military base, for an initial 99 years, for annual payments. The United States, India and the African Union welcomed it, while the Conservatives, Reform UK and some Chagossians objected. On 16 February 2026 four Chagossians, accompanied by a former Conservative member of parliament, landed without permits on Île du Coin in the Peros Banhos atoll, intending to settle. The territory's Chief Justice blocked their removal, and on 31 March 2026 he quashed the 2004 rule that no person has a right to live in the territory. He also held that the group was on the island illegally and had gained no right to a permanent camp. His decision was put on hold during an appeal heard on 15 to 17 July 2026, and six Chagossians were still living on the island in September.

Ratification stalled that year, as Britain said a change in the American president's position prevented updating the 1966 British and American agreement. The implementing bill lapsed in April 2026. In March Mauritius had said it was exploring legal avenues over the delay. In September the new British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said he would work towards a resolution, and the Defence Secretary said Britain would not make the agreed payments at this stage. On 13 October a Foreign Office minister told the House of Lords that an agreement must protect UK interests and command US support, and that the government would return to the bill in due course. As of mid-October 2026 the treaty had been signed and had not entered into force.
chagos-treaty-2025.why: Brought up to mid-October 2026 and gave the outcome of the Île du Coin landing.

bay-mills-vanderbilt.story:
The Bay Mills Indian Community runs a casino on its reservation under a compact with Michigan, which is what federal gaming law requires for casino games on Indian lands. In 2010 it opened a second gaming site in Vanderbilt, a small village in Michigan's Lower Peninsula about 125 miles from the reservation. It bought the property with interest from a federal fund that Congress had created to compensate the tribe for 19th-century takings of land, and it argued that this purchase made the property Indian land. The Interior Department concluded that it did not, and Michigan sued to close the casino. A federal judge ordered it closed in 2011. The Sixth Circuit appeals court later threw out that order, finding that the lower court lacked jurisdiction over some claims and that the tribe had immunity.

In 2014 the United States Supreme Court ruled for the tribe on immunity, though not on the land. The gaming law removes immunity only for gaming on Indian lands, and the state's own case was that this casino was off them, so no exception applied. The Court also refused to overturn its earlier decision in Kiowa, which had extended immunity to off-reservation business. It said that limiting the immunity is the job of Congress.

The Court pointed out what the state could still do. On its own land a state has more power, it said, and it can bring actions against the responsible individuals. The opinion is the clearest statement of how much protection a tribal partner can bring and where the protection stops. The state's right to pursue people, and to enforce its law on its own land, continues even when it cannot sue the tribe.

Winning on immunity did not reopen the casino. In September 2018 it was still closed, the case over the status of the land was still in court, and a tribal spokesman said the tribe would not reopen until it won at trial. What has happened to the site since then is not known.
bay-mills-vanderbilt.why: Status said operating, but the casino closed under the 2011 order and was still closed in 2018. Added the injunction and the aftermath.

add_sources.t: Court says Bay Mills casino can reopen, WNMU-FM, 28 May 2014
Fate of Closed Michigan Tribal Casino Rests With Courts, GGB Magazine, 9 Sep 2018

big-picture-loans.story:
The Lac Vieux Desert Band of Lake Superior Chippewa Indians entered online lending in 2011 through a tribally owned company, Red Rock Lending, with help from a company owned by an outside investor, Matt Martorello. After an adverse Second Circuit ruling and a federal enforcement action against another lender claiming tribal ties, the tribe restructured the business into Big Picture Loans and Ascension Technologies and bought Martorello's company in a seller-financed deal. Under it the tribe first received 2 percent of gross revenue, later 3 percent. By September 2017 about $20 million had gone to a company connected to the investor and nearly $5 million to the tribe.

Virginia borrowers sued, saying the loans broke state law. A district court found that the structure was set up mainly to help the investor avoid liability and denied immunity. On 3 July 2019 the Fourth Circuit reversed. It agreed that the company claiming immunity must prove it, and it adopted factors on creation, purpose, control, intent and financial relationship. It said there is no rule that a tribe must get a set share of revenue, and it held both companies to be arms of the tribe. Federal court records later included a finding, reported in 2020, that facts had been misrepresented to the Fourth Circuit.

The case then continued against the investor. The tribe, Big Picture Loans and Ascension Technologies reached a nationwide settlement with the borrowers. Martorello fought on, and on 16 July 2025 the Fourth Circuit ruled against him in Williams v. Martorello. It held that the settled tribal parties did not have to be in the case, that Virginia's 12 percent limit on interest governed internet loans it treated as made off the reservation, and that a person sued under the federal racketeering law for collecting unlawful debt cannot defend himself by saying he did not know the debt was illegal. It affirmed a judgment of $43,401,817.47 for a class of 491,018 borrowers.

The Second Circuit took a different path in Gingras v. Think Finance on 24 April 2019. There a tribe's officers could be sued for orders stopping violations of state law off tribal land, and the loans' arbitration clauses were found unenforceable. The two rulings are about different claims, so they do not directly clash, and together they show what a tribal partnership can and cannot cover.
big-picture-loans.why: Outcome missing: tribal settlement and the 2025 ruling affirming a $43.4 million judgment against the investor. Taken from a secondary commentary because the opinion copy returned 403.

add_sources.t: CaseMine commentary on Williams v. Martorello (4th Cir. 16 Jul 2025)

saint-regis-allergan.story:
Restasis is an eye drug made by Allergan. Its patents protected it from cheaper copies, and a competitor, Mylan, challenged them at the United States Patent and Trademark Office through a process called inter partes review, in which a panel of the Office looks again at a patent it granted. Before the hearing, Allergan and the Saint Regis Mohawk Tribe of northern New York made an agreement, which Mylan said was meant to shield the patents from review. On 8 September 2017 an assignment transferring the patents to the tribe was recorded. The tribe then moved to end the review on the ground of its sovereign immunity, and Allergan moved to withdraw. The panel refused both.

On 20 July 2018 the Federal Circuit, the appeals court for patent cases, ruled against the tribe. Tribes are immune from suits brought by private parties, the court said, and they are not immune from action by the federal government. It reasoned that the review resembled an agency enforcement action more than a private civil suit, because the director of the Office has wide discretion on whether to start one and the panel can continue even if the parties leave. The Office was acting as a superior sovereign reconsidering its own grant. The court decided only that point, and it left for another day whether a state's immunity is any different. The Supreme Court later denied the tribe's request to hear the case. On 14 June 2019, in Regents of the University of Minnesota v. LSI, the Federal Circuit answered the open question and held that a state's immunity does not stop such a review either, relying heavily on its Saint Regis decision.

The patents also lost in a different court. On 16 October 2017, in a separate case against the drug maker Teva, Judge William Bryson held the Restasis patents invalid as obvious. He also questioned whether a deal of this kind was the sort of transaction that tribal immunity was meant to cover.

The case shows that placing an asset with a sovereign partner does not move it out of reach of the federal government that created the right.
saint-regis-allergan.why: The question the text left open was answered in 2019 (state immunity also fails). Added the denied petition and the 2017 invalidity ruling on the patents.

add_sources.t: Federal Circuit confirms that state sovereign immunity, like tribal immunity, cannot shield patents, Mondaq, 1 Jul 2019
Judge Rules Restasis Patents Invalid, Center for Biosimilars, 18 Oct 2017

kthy-northern-cyprus-flights.story:
In November 2006 the airline Kibris Turk Hava Yollari, or KTHY, and a holiday company applied to Britain for permission to fly directly between the United Kingdom and Ercan airport in Northern Cyprus. The court described KTHY as a Turkish airline. It had flown between Britain and Turkey since 1999. Northern Cyprus declared independence in 1983, UN Security Council resolutions 541 and 550 called the declaration invalid and asked states not to recognise it, and only Turkey has done so.

Britain refused, and the companies sued. The High Court judge, Wyn Williams J, held that under the Chicago Convention, the treaty on civil flying, the Republic of Cyprus has exclusive sovereignty over the air above the whole island, including the north where it has no control. Article 6 says scheduled flights into a state's territory need that state's permission, and Cyprus had refused. A permit from Britain would therefore breach the treaty.

On appeal in 2010 the companies argued that a treaty must be read realistically, and that rights over territory lapse when a government loses effective control. They pointed to the principle in the International Court of Justice's Namibia opinion, that non-recognition should not deprive people of the benefits of international cooperation. The Court of Appeal rejected the argument on the Convention and dismissed the appeal.

It found no need to take the recognition point further. The case is the leading illustration of how the air treaty treats a place without recognition. Practical control of an airport did not give access to the air routes of the world, and the recognised state's rights survived a long loss of control. The ruling binds English courts only. The airline had already collapsed by then. With about $100 million of debt, it stopped flying on 21 June 2010 and was declared bankrupt on 19 September, around the time of the Court of Appeal's judgment of 12 October 2010.
kthy-northern-cyprus-flights.why: Outcome added: the airline collapsed before the appeal judgment.

starbase-texas.story:
Starbase is a city on the Texas Gulf coast around SpaceX's rocket site at Boca Chica. Elon Musk announced plans for a city called Starbase in March 2021. The Cameron County judge, Eddie Treviño Jr., said that SpaceX must follow all state incorporation rules. A petition to incorporate went to the county in 2024, and voters approved it on 3 May 2025. The city was formed on 20 May 2025 as a Type C general city, with a mayor and two commissioners, and had about 500 people.

Bobby Peden, a SpaceX vice-president, ran unopposed for mayor, and two other residents with ties to SpaceX filled the commission seats without opposition. On 3 February 2026 the commission approved a city police department, and in 2026 the city was planning to annex 7,133 acres of unpopulated land, which would bring the city to about 8,000 acres.

Nothing in this is outside ordinary state law. A group of residents followed the state's normal procedure for making a city, and the ties of its officials to one employer did not change the procedure. Federal aviation and environmental law, state law and county roads all remain. The case is the current American example of the simplest form of the idea, in which an employer's workers live in one place and vote themselves into a municipality.
starbase-texas.why: The listed source says the annexation was planned, and does not say a vote approved it. Worded to match.

international-seabed-authority.story:
About half of the world's ocean area lies over seabed that belongs to no country. Its floor holds metal-rich nodules and other mineral deposits. The 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea calls this seabed the common heritage of all mankind, and it sets up an international body to run it, the International Seabed Authority. The authority is based in Kingston, Jamaica, and held its first meeting there on 16 November 1994, the day the treaty took effect. It has 172 members, 171 countries and the European Union, and is funded by members and mining contractors. The United States has not ratified the treaty and is not a member.

It works differently from a land claim. Nobody can own this seabed by finding or occupying it. A company that wants to mine there needs two things, a contract with the authority and the backing of a member country, called a sponsor. The sponsor answers for the company's conduct. So a small country can sponsor a company, as Nauru and Tonga have, and it is the country that gives the company its way in.

The authority has two jobs that pull against each other. It authorises mining and it is also supposed to protect the seabed environment. Since 1994 it has approved more than two dozen exploration contracts in the Atlantic, Pacific and Indian Oceans, most of them in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone between Hawaii and Mexico, where nodules contain copper, cobalt and other metals used in batteries. It has not approved any commercial mining. It is still writing the rules, while scientists and environmental groups warn of harm to the ocean and call for a pause.

The politics sharpened in 2026. The council met in March without finishing the mining rules, leaving benefit-sharing, liability and environmental compensation unresolved. The authority opened an inquiry into whether two contractors, NORI and TOML, had broken their obligations by seeking American mining permits. On 18 July 2026 a specialist chamber of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea ordered the authority to respect due process, meaning fair procedure, in that inquiry. Two days later the council extended NORI's exploration contract to 2031.

For anyone thinking of founding something on the seabed, the rule is plain. Under this treaty the bottom of the sea past national zones cannot be taken, and the only legal route to its minerals is a contract through this body. Countries outside the treaty, such as the United States, are the main open question. According to The Metals Company's report of the July 2026 session, the United States told the authority that it is not a party, that it is not bound by the treaty's seabed mining rules and that it does not regard those rules as customary law, meaning rules binding on every state whether it joined or not. The authority's members treat the seabed regime as binding among themselves, and no court has ruled on the American position.
international-seabed-authority.why: The open question now has a stated US position; said who argues what.

add_sources.t: TMC Provides Second Quarter 2026 Corporate Update, via Finviz

metals-company.story:
The Metals Company is a Canadian-founded business that wants to mine metal-rich nodules from the Pacific floor. It began as DeepGreen Metals in 2011. The nodules, which contain nickel, copper, cobalt and manganese, lie in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, about 1,500 miles southwest of San Diego, on seabed that no country owns. Under the Law of the Sea treaty, that seabed is controlled by the International Seabed Authority, and a company needs a contract with the authority and a sponsoring member country.

The company worked within that system by using small Pacific states. Its subsidiary NORI held an exploration contract sponsored by Nauru, and it later bought TOML, sponsored by Tonga. In 2012 DeepGreen agreed to sell 50 percent of its future nickel and copper from the NORI area to the commodity trader Glencore. In 2021 it merged with a listed shell company, a firm with a stock listing and no business, in a $2.9 billion deal, and took its current name.

In June 2021 Nauru told the authority that it intended to begin mining. A rule in the treaty system meant that this started a two-year deadline to finish the mining rules. The deadline passed and the rules were not finished, which left the company with exploration rights and no way to mine.

It then turned to another route. The United States never joined the treaty, and it has its own older law on seabed mining. On 24 April 2025 President Trump signed an order telling the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the American ocean agency, to speed up permits under that law. Within days the company's American arm applied. NOAA published its application for public comment in August 2026, and no permit had been issued by that month. In its second-quarter 2026 report the company said NOAA's review had slipped by a few months and that it still expected the permit before commissioning its offshore collection system, targeted for the end of 2027.

The authority responded by opening an inquiry into whether NORI and TOML had broken their contracts. The two companies took it to a specialist chamber of the international law of the sea tribunal in June 2026, and on 18 July the chamber ordered the authority to respect fair procedure, without suspending the inquiry. The main case is undecided. NORI's contract was extended to 2031, and TOML's runs to January 2027 with an extension pending.

The company stands on both sides of the question. Its subsidiaries hold contracts under the treaty, and its American arm seeks a permit that would bypass that treaty. The United States told the authority in July 2026, by the company's account, that it is not bound by the treaty's seabed mining rules. What remains open is whether one country's permit can give a company a right to mine an area that most of the world has agreed to manage together. The answer will affect anyone hoping to operate outside the shared system with one government's approval.
metals-company.why: 'Four days' not supported (reported 29 April, five days after the order). Added the company's August 2026 statement on the permit timing and the US position.

add_sources.t: TMC Provides Second Quarter 2026 Corporate Update, via Finviz

network-state-school.story:
The Network State is an idea for starting new countries online, and the Network School is its test site. Balaji Srinivasan, former chief technology officer of the cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase, set out the idea in a 2022 book. An online community forms first around shared values, it pools money to buy land in scattered places, and it eventually seeks diplomatic recognition from real governments. This reverses the usual order, in which land comes first.

In August 2024 he announced the Network School in a hotel at Forest City, a half-empty development in Johor, Malaysia. It became permanent in May 2025. It was a private community where startup founders, engineers and other tech workers lived and worked together, paying about $1,500 to $3,000 a month. It was not a government-recognised university and gave no degrees. Srinivasan said over $100 million was committed to it. In law it was an ordinary business with a council licence, run in Malaysia under Malaysian licensing and immigration rules.

Then came trouble. Social media claims spread that Israelis had entered on second passports, a charged issue in Malaysia. Malaysian officers inspected the site on 14 July 2026, checked 266 foreigners from 40 countries and found all documents valid. Commentators also objected to its stated aims on sovereignty and asked how it came to operate there at all. Srinivasan suspended a planned $500 million investment. On 21 July the Iskandar Puteri City Council revoked the school's business licence, citing breaches of licence conditions and of how the premises could be used, and ordered it to stop the next day.

Within hours Kazakhstan's digital ministry signed a memorandum, a non-binding statement of intent, to host a campus. Network School Kazakhstan launched at a centre in Astana on 2 September 2026, with Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev taking part. In October 2026 the Kazakh publication Digital Business reported that the project was moving its headquarters to Astana under the memorandum, with its members going to a campus at the Alem.ai international AI centre, and that it was raising money at a valuation of $2 billion in a round involving Andreessen Horowitz and Coinbase.

The episode gave the idea a real test. A community can begin online, but once it has rooms and residents it needs a host country, and a city council's ordinary licensing power was enough to close it in one day. Having money and members did not change that. The move shows the other side of the same position. A mobile community can leave for a government that wants it, and it will then live under that government's rules.

add_sources.t: Astana is the next Dubai, Digital Business (Kazakhstan), 12 Oct 2026

order-of-malta.story:
The Sovereign Military Order of Malta is the oldest and best-known answer to a question that runs through this whole subject, which is whether something can be sovereign without land. Sovereign means treated as an independent authority in international law, able to deal with states as an equal. The Order is a Catholic religious order with 39 vowed members and no territory of its own, and many countries treat it that way.

It began in the 11th century as a hospital community in Jerusalem, founded by a man known as Blessed Gerard, and Pope Paschal II approved it in 1113. As the Crusades went on it became a military order as well. It later ruled the island of Rhodes and then Malta, which it defended for more than three months against the Ottoman Empire in the Great Siege of 1565. For those centuries it was an ordinary territorial state.

In June 1798 Napoleon's forces took Malta and the Order lost its last territory. Then something unusual happened. Other countries went on treating it as a sovereign body, and it kept conducting diplomacy from its new base. It holds two headquarters buildings in Rome with extraterritorial status, meaning that Italian law treats them as outside normal Italian control, though they are not a territory the Order rules as a country. It also has a treaty with Malta, signed on 5 December 1998 and ratified in 2001, that lets it use the upper part of Fort St. Angelo in Birgu with limited extraterritoriality for 99 years. The fort stays under Malta's sovereignty, Malta may end the treaty after 50 years, the Order may not grant asylum there and Maltese courts generally keep full jurisdiction. So the one place on Malta it uses again comes by permission of the state that holds the island.

Day to day it does what a state's foreign ministry does. It issues its own passports, coins and stamps, and it signs treaties. Its website reports diplomatic relations with 118 countries and the European Union, while Wikipedia gives 115 states. The United Nations General Assembly made it a permanent observer in 1994, citing its humanitarian work. Only three of its senior officers count as its citizens, so no population depends on it. The rest of its members are citizens of ordinary countries. It says its diplomatic network exists to give its medical programmes protected access in crisis regions, and its hospitals and aid work supply the reason for states to keep the relationship going.

People who want a state without land often point to the Order. Its case is hard to copy. Its status rests on some nine centuries of history, on having once really ruled territory, on the Catholic Church's support and on a stream of aid work that governments value. Its recognition was inherited from a time when it held land, and no group has been shown to gain the same treatment from scratch. It shows that diplomatic recognition can outlast territory, as long as enough states choose to continue it.
order-of-malta.why: Added the Fort St. Angelo treaty, the closest thing the Order has to territory today, which the entry omitted. In the entry's listed Wikipedia page.

tuvalu-digital-nation.story:
Tuvalu is a recognised Pacific country of about 10,000 people, spread over low-lying islands that the United Nations Development Programme classes as extremely vulnerable to climate change. The Rising Nations Initiative says that small island nations such as Tuvalu, Kiribati and the Marshall Islands are likely to become uninhabitable within a few decades. That raises a question international law has never had to answer, which is what happens to a country when its land goes under water.

The usual test for a state, set out in the 1933 Montevideo Convention, asks for a permanent population, a defined territory, a government and the ability to deal with other states. Territory is on that list. So on one reading Tuvalu could lose its legal existence along with its homes. At the COP27 climate conference in November 2022 its Foreign Minister, Simon Kofe, appeared in a video standing knee deep in the ocean.

He said the country would move its land, ocean and culture to the cloud, as what it called the first digital nation. The plan, part of the Future Now Project, is to map all 124 islands and islets and to record cultural objects, language, elders' stories and dances, so that people abroad and future generations can keep them. The legal step is the more important one.

Tuvalu has asked other countries to agree in advance that it stays a state whatever happens to its land. Australia's Law Society Journal reported that 26 countries, including New Zealand and Australia, had legally recognised its digital statehood by December 2023, with a goal of 50. Australia also offered residency to 280 Tuvaluans a year, under the Falepili Union, a treaty between the two countries signed on 9 November 2023 that entered into force on 28 August 2024. In its climate advisory opinion of July 2025 the International Court of Justice, the United Nations' top court, said that the disappearance of one of a state's parts "would not necessarily entail the loss of its statehood".

An advisory opinion does not bind states, though it carries weight. The land is still there and the question has not been tested. The case differs from every self-declared internet nation in one way. Tuvalu starts as a full state with UN membership and is seeking to keep that status, so the digital record is a supplement to recognition it already has. Its strategy shows where the law's flexibility lies.

States may be able to preserve a state by agreement, and this does not open the door for a new one to be created online.
tuvalu-digital-nation.why: Named the treaty and gave its entry into force.

mcclean-rockall.story:
Rockall is a bare granite rock about 17 metres high in the North Atlantic, 301 kilometres west of the Scottish island of Soay, and it is uninhabitable. Britain claimed it in 1955 and made it part of Scotland in 1972. Ireland has never claimed the rock itself but disputes Britain's position.

Why anyone would care comes down to what a rock can generate at sea. Under the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, the main treaty on ocean rights, a country's land gives it an exclusive economic zone, a belt of sea up to 200 nautical miles wide where it controls fish and minerals, and rights over the nearby seabed, called the continental shelf. But a rock that cannot support human life or economic activity of its own gets neither. So in the 1980s it could seem that whether people can live on Rockall would decide who controls a large area of sea.

Tom McClean set out to help Britain's side of that question. Abandoned as a baby in Dublin and raised at first in an orphanage, he served in Britain's Parachute Regiment and Special Air Service and became a survival expert. He is the opposite of a breakaway founder, because he went to reinforce an existing state's claim. He lived on the rock from 26 May to 4 July 1985, in what one account calls a wooden box, a record 40 days alone.

The claim that his stay reaffirmed Britain's title has been questioned, and a single person with supplies brought in does not show that a place can support human life. The record did not stand. Greenpeace activists passed it in 1997 with 42 days, and Nick Hancock reached 45 days alone in 2014. Britain's position later moved away from the argument he was supporting. Its 1988 boundary agreement with Ireland had already said that the rock's location was irrelevant, and it ratified the treaty on 25 July 1997. In 2012 its Foreign Office said that it reads the treaty to give Rockall no economic zone or continental shelf, only a 12-nautical-mile belt of territorial sea, which lies inside Britain's wider zones. Ireland says rocks of this kind should have no significance for claims to the seabed, and it does not recognise British sovereignty over the rock. McClean's stay shows how far people will go to give a rock legal weight, and Britain itself no longer claims the wide zones from it.
mcclean-rockall.why: The story implied habitability still decides the sea area. Britain's own stated reading since 1997 and 2012 is that Rockall generates only 12 nautical miles. In the listed Rockall page.

waveland-rockall.story:
Rockall is a small granite rock in the North Atlantic, about 301 kilometres from the nearest Scottish island of Soay. Britain claimed it in 1955 and made it part of Scotland in 1972. Ireland, Iceland and Denmark have contested the rights around it, because the surrounding seabed may hold oil.

The environmental group Greenpeace chose it for that reason. In the mid-1990s it was campaigning against oil exploration in the Atlantic, including a £1 billion field run by the oil company BP, and BP was at the same time seeking to sue four of its members for £1.4 million over an earlier protest. On 11 June 1997 activists landed on the rock. Three or four at a time stayed for 42 days, a record then.

They declared Rockall the capital of the Global State of Waveland and offered citizenship to anyone who would take a pledge of allegiance. It was a protest in the form of a country. John Vidal, one of those who landed, said the team unscrewed the 1955 British plaque and refixed it back to front. The Flags of the World website says that Prime Minister Tony Blair refused their petition for recognition.

The British government's reply was the most instructive part. It said that Rockall was British territory and that anyone was free to go there and stay as long as they pleased. By treating the occupiers as ordinary visitors on British soil, it never had to act against them or take the claim seriously. No force was used. Greenpeace used the occupation as a base for actions against rigs and ships surveying for oil, and landed again in 1998.

On 25 July 1997, days after the occupation ended, Britain ratified the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, under which a rock that cannot support human habitation or economic life gets no economic zone or continental shelf. Britain's Foreign Office said in 2012 that it reads this to give Rockall only a 12-nautical-mile territorial sea. So the seabed dispute now rests on the wider continental shelf claims of the four countries and not on who holds the rock. Waveland has no standing in any country's law, and Britain still holds Rockall. The episode shows that declaring a state can succeed as publicity, and that a government can defeat the legal claim simply by ignoring it.
waveland-rockall.why: Holding the rock does not give the seabed under the treaty and Britain's stated reading; corrected, using the listed Rockall page.

bakov-arca-noe.story:
Anton Bakov is a Russian businessman and former member of Russia's parliament who chairs the Monarchist Party. He is known for a long series of unusual political projects, including a local currency called the Ural franc. In 2011 he founded a project to restore the Russian Empire, overthrown in 1917, as a small state somewhere outside Russia.

Under the name Imperial Throne it issued a manifesto on 31 March 2014 naming a German prince, Karl Emich of Leiningen, as Emperor Nicholas III, with Bakov as prime minister and later Archchancellor. It took the name Romanov Empire in 2017. It sold passports online for 1,000 rubles, about 31 American dollars, and claimed about 4,000 by 2014. In 2013 it said it had given citizenship to Edward Snowden, the American who leaked secret surveillance files.

Because a state needs land and it had none, its leaders went shopping. Nicholas III asked Vladimir Putin for land in Yekaterinburg and was refused. Bakov held talks to buy territory from Kiribati and the Gambia, and these had failed by 2017.

In 2020 Bakov announced a successor project called Arca Noë, to be based in what he called neutral Mediterranean waters close to Venice, as part of the seasteading movement, which aims to build permanent homes at sea. No structure has been reported. In January 2025 Bakov told the media that he had set up an international organisation, the Union of Gaza Developers, and was negotiating to become a contractor for rebuilding the Gaza Strip.

The search shows the usual progress of a claim without land. It starts with asking governments, and after they refuse it moves to open water, where no state's consent seems necessary, and building there has its own costs. So the project remains a title, a set of passports and a plan.
bakov-arca-noe.why: Later activity added from the listed page.

xlii-seastead-phuket.story:
A seastead is a permanent home at sea, and its backers hope to live beyond any country's laws. XLII was a small one, a six-metre-wide cabin raised on a weighted column, paid for and built by a company called Ocean Builders. It was anchored in the Andaman Sea about 14 nautical miles off Phuket, Thailand. Chad Elwartowski, a 46-year-old American bitcoin trader, and his Thai partner Supranee Thepdet moved in during early 2019.

The location was chosen with the law of the sea in mind. A country's full territorial sea ends 12 nautical miles from its coast. From 12 to 24 miles is the contiguous zone, where it has only limited powers such as customs enforcement. Out to 200 miles is the exclusive economic zone, where it controls fish and minerals. Ocean Builders and its supporters relied on the limits these rules place on a coastal state past 12 miles. Elwartowski said 20 more homes would be sold to form a community.

Thailand disagreed. The Thai navy said that the couple had announced autonomy beyond the reach of any court and invited others to join, and it treated this as an attack on the country's sovereignty, its right to rule its own territory. The couple left before the navy raided the cabin on 13 April 2019. Thailand revoked Elwartowski's visa and charged the two under a law carrying life in prison or death. On 22 April navy boats began towing the cabin to shore as evidence.

Ocean Builders said that the cabin sat in the contiguous zone and that no micronation was intended. Thailand pointed to its 200-mile economic zone. A senior official urged the couple to come back and fight the charge in court. The charge was under Section 119 of the Criminal Code, on threats to national security. In June 2019 officials said there had been no progress in arresting them, after tracing them to Tarutao island in April. Police had twice asked the couple to present themselves to be formally told of the charge, and they had not done so. On 17 June Elwartowski said on Facebook that the two had married. In July prosecutors said nine more suspects would be charged, among them seven Thais and a German. No court outcome in Thailand is known. The couple were not caught, and the Seasteading Institute wrote in 2024 that they had gone on to build seasteads again in Panama.

The treaty does limit what a state may do past 12 miles, but a state that sees a threat can act first and argue later, and those living on the platform carried the risk. Their case also shows the problem of ties to land, since Thepdet was a Thai citizen and Elwartowski held a Thai visa, and that gave Thailand direct power over them whatever the status of the water.
xlii-seastead-phuket.why: Added the statute, the formal state of the charge in June 2019 and what became of the couple. No ruling found.

cheran.story:
Cherán is a town of the Indigenous Purépecha people in the state of Michoacán, in western Mexico. Its economy rests on timber, and Mexico's cartels had moved into logging. For more than three years armed loggers and masked men demanding money from small businesses worked there without being punished, and killings and kidnappings became routine. Trucks full of cut logs passed through the town day after day. By 2011 the loggers were getting close to one of the town's water springs, and water was what finally moved people.

A group of local women met in secret. They decided to stop the trucks in town, where neighbours could back them up. When they did, on 15 April 2011, the uprising drove out the loggers, the police and the politicians.

Then the town had to run itself. Political parties were banned, and they were still banned when the BBC visited five years later. Each of the four districts elected representatives to a ruling council. Armed checkpoints went up on the three main roads, staffed by the Ronda Comunitaria, a local force of men and women who stop every vehicle and question those inside.

The important legal step came next. The community asked to choose its authorities by its own customs, and on 2 November 2011 Mexico's federal Electoral Tribunal ordered Michoacán's electoral authority and state congress to act on that request. The court's order turned a local uprising into an arrangement that the state had to deal with. On 22 January 2012 the community elected its High Council of Communal Government by custom, and the state's electoral institute validated the election.

The council then used the courts itself. In March 2012 Michoacán changed its constitution on Indigenous matters without consulting the community, and the council sued. On 29 May 2014 Mexico's Supreme Court ruled for it, holding that Indigenous peoples have a right to be consulted in such a law-making process, and declared the reform invalid with effect only for the parties to the case. The Third Council was named in 2018. The town is now described as a self-ruling Indigenous community largely free of the crime and corruption that caused the revolt.

Cherán does not claim to be a separate country. That is a large part of why it survives. It asked to be governed differently within Mexico, on the grounds of existing rights, and it won that in a Mexican court. It offers a contrast with many declared states. It has real land, real residents and real day-to-day control, and it did not need a flag or passport to get them.
cheran.why: Added the date of the rising, the 2012 election and the 2014 Supreme Court ruling, a major later outcome.

add_sources.t: Mexico Supreme Court, Controversia Constitucional 32/2012, official summary

difc.story:
Many people who want a separate legal territory actually want better commercial law and lower tax. The Dubai International Financial Centre (DIFC) shows a government providing exactly that. It is a 110-hectare business district in Dubai, one of the emirates that make up the United Arab Emirates, with its own commercial law and courts.

Its creators wanted to attract international finance, and bankers and investors prefer legal systems they know. In September 2004 a federal law allowed each emirate to set up legal structures for financial centres. Dubai Law No. 9 of 2004 then created the centre, and Dubai Law No. 12 created its courts, which began working in 2006. Dubai Law No. 5 of 2021 fully replaced the 2004 founding law from 27 April 2021. Inside the zone, civil and commercial cases follow common law, the English system built on past court rulings, in English, separately from the rest of the country's legal system.

It also has its own financial regulator and offers companies a 50-year guarantee of zero tax on corporate income. Other laws, such as criminal law and immigration rules, still apply there. So a banker in the DIFC can sign a contract governed by the zone's commercial law, but if arrested for assault is dealt with under the national criminal system.

At first the courts could hear only cases tied to the zone. A law of 31 October 2011 let them hear any local or international commercial case if all parties agree, so firms with no link to the zone can also use them. In effect the courts became a service open to anyone who chooses them.

The zone remains part of Dubai, and its courts are part of the emirate's own structure. Its powers come from statutes, so they can be changed by further statutes, and the 2021 replacement of its founding law is an example. No one here claims independence. The case shows how far a country can go in carving out a separate legal system, and shows that the carving is done by the country.
difc.why: The 2004 founding law was replaced in 2021; the entry read as if it still governs.

add_sources.t: The issuance of Law No. 5 of 2021, Al Tamimi & Company
